edits.old: For the demonstrated two-compartment neuronal device, the single-unit photomask places two culture wells on opposite sides of 62 parallel microchannels with a design width of 10 µm and 30 µm interchannel gaps (Fig. 1B). The SU-8 channel features and SUEX well bases and alignment openings are represented as distinct coordinated mask layers. Repetition of the unit at 18 × 9 mm spacing produced a wafer-scale layout comprising 48 two-compartment devices in a 6 × 8 array, with 96 wells on a standard 9 mm plate grid (Fig. 1C). The corresponding insert models depict the two well-forming structures required for one device and their placement in the complete 96-insert array (Fig. 1D). OpenMFD also generated the matching plate-frame model (Fig. 1E). The assembled microfluidic plate shown in Fig. 1F demonstrates the physical plate format obtained from this coordinated design.

edits.old: The principal device comprised a 6 × 8 array of 48 two-compartment microfluidic units containing 96 wells on a standard 9 mm grid. Each device incorporated 62 microchannels with a nominal width of 10 µm and 30 µm interchannel gaps. A horizontal scaling factor of 1.0226 was applied to matching fabrication files to compensate for polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) shrinkage during curing at 100 °C. Additional designs were generated for oligodendrocyte myelination, orthogonal-gradient axon guidance, and three-compartment neuronal culture configurations. Design dimensions are provided in Table S1 within Supplementary Protocol 1, and alternative design geometries are summarized in Fig. 2 and the OpenMFD repository.

edits.old: Hybrid mold fabrication - Reusable hybrid molds were fabricated on 6-inch silicon wafers by combining photolithographically patterned SU-8 and SUEX photoresists with 3D-printed resin inserts (Fig. 3). The photolithographic structures comprised two nominally 5 µm layers of SU-8 2005 (Kayaku Advanced Materials) and a 200 µm layer of SUEX K200 dry-film photoresist (DJ MicroLaminates). The first SU-8 layer was uniformly exposed to form a continuous base beneath the microchannel features. A second SU-8 layer was patterned through the microchannel photomask, developed, and baked at 150 °C for 10 min before SUEX lamination. The SUEX layer defined the well bases and alignment openings and was exposed through an LP360 long-pass filter. Complete photolithographic processing parameters are provided in Supplementary Protocol 1.

edits.old: Simultaneous bonding required accommodation of variation in the heights of the printed inserts. Measurements across one 96-position array showed a mean pin height of 5.551 mm, a standard deviation of 26.7 µm, and a total range of 116 µm (5.483–5.599 mm; Fig. 3G; Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S1). Rigid clamping did not provide uniform contact across the array. Incorporating a compressible ethylene propylene diene monomer (EPDM) backing into the clamping assembly accommodated differences in insert height and enabled collective seating of the alignment pins within their corresponding SUEX openings (Fig. 3C,D). Following adhesive curing, the flexible printing plate could be separated from the bonded inserts, leaving the array attached to the patterned silicon wafer (Fig. 3E). The patterned SUEX features and alignment openings before insert attachment are shown in Fig. 3F.

edits.old: The insert-height measurements in Fig. 3G identify an important constraint on collective assembly: across 96 positions, mean pin height was 5.551 mm, with a standard deviation of 26.7 µm and a 116 µm range. Rigid clamping did not provide uniform contact, whereas a compressible EPDM backing accommodated height variation during bonding. Square pins and corresponding SUEX openings provided a nominal 75 µm clearance per side, allowing registration without individual insert positioning. These results support the practicality of array transfer, but they do not quantify final alignment error or compare bonding yield statistically between clamping methods. The SU-8 base layer, pre-SUEX bake, and filtered SUEX exposure likewise reflect process-development solutions to observed adhesion and surface-flatness problems rather than independently controlled optimization studies.

edits.old: The reusable hybrid molds were used to cast complete polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) microfluidic arrays in which the integrated resin inserts formed the culture wells directly (Fig. 4A). Each cast contained 48 two-compartment devices with 96 preformed well openings, eliminating the need to punch individual reservoirs after demolding (Fig. 4B). The well-forming inserts remained attached to the mold between production cycles, allowing subsequent plates to be cast without repeating photolithography, insert alignment, or insert bonding. Multiple filled molds could also be processed in parallel using the same wafer-rack arrangement.

edits.old: The released PDMS arrays were trimmed along their molded cutting guides and bonded to glass to produce optically accessible culture substrates (Fig. 4C). Incorporation of the glass-backed arrays into printed support frames produced complete plate-format devices (Fig. 4D). The final assemblies retained the designed 9 mm well grid and were compatible with standard plate handling. These steps converted the wafer-scale cast into a practical culture plate while leaving the microfluidic architecture defined by the reusable mold.

edits.old: To assess repeated manufacturing performance, we recorded the outcomes of five hybrid molds assembled using the optimized procedure (Fig. 4E). Three molds entered routine use and collectively produced more than 50 usable PDMS casts. Of the two remaining molds, one fractured during demolding and the other was lost when PDMS leaked beneath the wafer and cured within the wafer rack. The most recently fabricated molds remained in use for more than eight months without visible deterioration of their patterned structures or attached inserts. These observations support repeated mold use, although the available records do not establish a per-cast success rate or mold-specific lifetime distribution.

edits.old: The retained inserts generated all 96 wells during each PDMS cast, separating one-time cleanroom-based mold production from routine plate fabrication. Three molds collectively yielded more than 50 usable casts (Fig. 4E), and the most recent molds remained in use for over eight months without visible deterioration. A parylene C coating permitted demolding without additional silane release treatment and kept the printed resin and adhesive within the mold rather than the finished culture device. Parylene has previously been investigated as an anti-adhesion coating in PDMS double casting (DOI: 10.1016/j.sna.2012.09.024). Protective effects of parylene on resin-printed components have been demonstrated in other biological applications (PMID: 37534979), although coating performance and potential leaching were not separately quantified here. One wafer fractured during demolding and another mold was lost after PDMS leaked beneath the wafer; these distinct failures do not establish a common mechanism. Nor did the present experiments quantify per-mold casting yields, production time, or cost savings relative to other methods.

edits.old: The assembled microfluidic plates retained the standard 9 mm well-centre spacing defined by OpenMFD, allowing eight wells within a plate column to be filled simultaneously using a conventional multichannel pipette (Fig. 5A). Both the Opera Phenix Plus and ImageXpress Micro Confocal high-content imaging systems focused on and acquired images of the assembled arrays without custom plate handling or instrument modification. The Opera Phenix Plus was used for the fluorescent tracer and neuronal labeling measurements described below. Thus, the framed arrays were compatible with established liquid-handling and automated microscopy workflows without requiring changes to the plate architecture.

edits.old: Fluorescent tracer transport assay - Directional tracer redistribution was examined in 24 two-compartment devices. Alexa Fluor 568-conjugated secondary antibody (1:1000 in phosphate-buffered saline [PBS]) was introduced into the left compartment at 25 µL, while Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated secondary antibody (1:1000 in PBS) was introduced into the right compartment at 50 µL. Devices were imaged immediately after loading and following 72 h of incubation without replenishment or volume adjustment. Red and green fluorescence distributions were compared qualitatively between the two time points (Fig. 5B).

edits.old: We next examined tracer redistribution between the two compartments of 24 devices following unequal initial loading volumes (Fig. 5B). Alexa Fluor 568-conjugated antibody (red) was introduced into the left compartment at 25 µL and Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated antibody (green) into the right compartment at 50 µL. Immediately after loading, fluorescence was predominantly confined to the respective loading compartments. After 72 h without medium replenishment or volume adjustment, green fluorescence was visible in the initially lower-volume left compartments, whereas comparatively little red fluorescence had redistributed in the opposite direction. The observed pattern was consistent with net tracer transport in the direction of the initial hydrostatic volume difference. Because fluorescence was recorded only at the initial and final time points, neither the magnitude nor the persistence of fluid flow could be determined; continuous compartmental isolation over the 72 h interval was not established.

edits.old: We then assessed whether the devices supported compartmentalized primary neuronal culture and retrograde axonal labeling. Cortical neurons isolated from one embryonic day 18 rat embryo were distributed across three separately assembled plates and maintained for 11 days in vitro (DIV). At DIV10, Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated cholera toxin subunit B (CTB-647) was applied selectively to the distal compartments. CTB-positive neuronal cell bodies were observed in the somatic compartments 24 h later, consistent with axonal extension into the distal compartments, uptake of the tracer, and retrograde transport (Fig. 5C). Representative images from each plate are shown alongside the corresponding image-analysis outlines used to identify labeled cell bodies.

edits.old: Long-term neuronal growth was less consistent at the plate perimeter than in the interior devices. Quantitative analysis was therefore restricted to the 24 interior positions on each of the three plates, yielding 72 device-level observations. Five counts were excluded from descriptive summaries because inspection identified segmentation or cell-count artifacts; count magnitude alone was not an exclusion criterion. The resulting 67 analyzed devices comprised 22, 21, and 24 devices on Plates 1, 2, and 3, respectively (Fig. 5D; Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S5). Mean CTB-positive cell-body counts per device were 177.7 ± 43.7 for Plate 1, 269.3 ± 62.3 for Plate 2, and 203.6 ± 32.4 for Plate 3 (mean ± standard deviation). The individual device values and all five excluded observations are retained in Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S5, and displayed in Fig. 5D. These were baseline measurements acquired before axotomy in a dimethyl sulfoxide-only experiment. Because all cultures originated from the same embryo, the plates and devices represent technical replicates rather than independent biological preparations.

edits.old: The framed 48-device arrays accommodated multichannel pipetting and automated imaging on two high-content microscopy systems without instrument modification. Fluorescent tracer redistribution was consistent with transport in the direction of an initial hydrostatic volume difference, but two time points over 72 h could not establish flow rate, pressure stability, or sustained compartmental isolation. Compartmentalized neuronal cultures have also supported studies of axon-to-soma signaling and retrograde transport (PMIDs: 34190355; 36826992). In the present biological demonstration, selective distal application of CTB labeled cortical neuronal somata (Fig. 5C,D), supporting access to axons extending into the distal compartments rather than testing a particular axonal signaling mechanism. The 67 analyzed interior devices across three plates provided a device-level readout, but all neurons originated from one embryo. Thus, these findings demonstrate assay feasibility and within-preparation variability, not reproducibility across biological preparations or readiness for screening.

edits.old: A persistent manufacturing challenge is the integration of micrometer-scale channels with millimeter-scale, pipette-accessible culture reservoirs. Conventional polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) soft lithography readily replicates lithographically patterned microfeatures, but reservoirs are commonly opened individually after curing, increasing manual handling as device numbers grow. For compartmentalized neuronal cultures, microchannel dimensions must also remain suitable for selective neurite access and robust experimental performance (PMID: 36111641). Multiscale molding has addressed this mismatch: hybrid milled and hot-embossed masters enabled simultaneous replication of channels and larger reservoirs without punching (PMID: 20049640), including in neuron–glia co-culture devices (PMID: 22828584). Hybrid additive manufacturing has also combined photolithographic channel features with printed compartment structures to avoid manual post-processing (PMID: 32832365). Other microfluidic manufacturing strategies include CO2 laser-cut PDMS channels (DOI: 10.1109/COASE.2007.4341853) and rapidly fabricated optical-adhesive culture chips (PMID: 26657733). Micro-to-millimeter fabrication by combining 3D printing and photolithography has also been reported (DOI: 10.7567/1347-4065/ab09d0). Thus, multiscale fabrication and the elimination of reservoir punching are established; an important remaining objective is to coordinate customizable plate-scale geometries with efficient, repeatable mold assembly.

edits.old: Fig. 1. OpenMFD enables coordinated parametric design of microfluidic devices and their fabrication components. (A) OpenMFD generates matched photolithographic masks, three-dimensional (3D) resin-insert models, and supporting plate components from shared design parameters defining well and microchannel geometry, device spacing, array dimensions, and alignment features. A common scaling factor of 1.0226 compensates for anticipated polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) shrinkage during curing at 100 °C. (B) Single two-compartment device photomask showing the SU-8 microchannels (blue; 62 channels, 10 µm design width and 30 µm interchannel gaps) and SUEX well-base and alignment features (green). (C) Wafer-scale photomask containing 48 two-compartment devices arranged in a 6 × 8 array, with an enlarged view of the repeated device geometry. (D) Computer-aided design (CAD) models of the two well-forming resin inserts for an individual device and the complete 96-insert array. (E) CAD model of the supporting plate frame. (F) Photograph of the assembled microfluidic culture plate containing 96 wells on a standard 9 mm grid.
edits.new: Fig. 1. Shared device dimensions keep photomasks, well-forming inserts and a plate frame matched as the design changes. edits.old: Fig. 4. Reusable hybrid molds enable repeated casting and assembly of plate-format microfluidic culture devices. (A) Original fabrication schematics showing the completed mold and subsequent PDMS casting below the tops of the retained well-forming inserts. (B) Schematic of a demolded PDMS array containing 48 two-compartment devices and 96 open wells formed directly during casting. (C) Trimming of a released cast and preparation of the glass-backed array. (D) Assembly of the glass-backed PDMS array into a printed supporting frame (schematic), alongside an original photograph of an assembled plate. (E) Recorded manufacturing outcomes: five hybrid molds assembled, three entering routine use, and two lost following wafer fracture or PDMS leakage beneath the wafer. The three routinely used molds collectively produced more than 50 usable PDMS casts; the most recently fabricated molds remained usable for over eight months without visible deterioration. Panel E reports aggregate observations and does not represent per-mold casting yields. Panels A–D show the casting and plate-assembly workflow.
edits.new: Fig. 4. Reusable-mold casting and assembly of a framed PDMS culture plate. Numbers and connecting arrows give the processing order. (1) The parylene-coated hybrid mold carries the well-forming inserts. (2) Sylgard 184 PDMS, mixed at a 10:1 base:curing-agent ratio, is poured below the insert tops so that the wells remain open. (3) Filled molds are degassed together in a wafer rack until bubbles clear. (4) The loaded rack is heated at 100°C for 1 h. (5) The cured cast is peeled from the mold, starting at the corners. (6) With its channel side facing upward, the cast is held flat with masking tape and trimmed along molded cutting guides to 108 × 72 mm. (7) The PDMS is plasma-bonded to a 110 × 74 × 0.17 mm glass sheet. After inspecting the seal, the bonded assembly is autoclaved at 121°C for 15 min. (8) The bonded array is seated glass-side up in an inverted HIPS frame containing LOCTITE SI 5140 silicone adhesive. (9) After a 3-day room-temperature adhesive cure, the plate is turned upright and receives a second plasma treatment before aqueous coating and culture (Supplementary Protocol 2; mold fabrication in Supplementary Protocol 1).

design_rows: 6 × 8 two-well units: 48 devices and 96 wells. Unit spacing: 18 × 9 mm; well centres: ±4.5 mm from each unit centre, on a 9 mm grid.
108 × 72 mm device; 110 × 74 mm glass, with a designed 1 mm margin per side; 150 mm wafer with a 57.5 mm flat.
2.5 mm well radius; 5.0 mm chamber width; 62 channels, 10 µm wide with 30 µm gaps. Channel-array width: 2.45 mm; chamber margin: 1.275 mm per side.
5 µm patterned SU-8 over a flood-exposed base; 200 µm SUEX wells and alignment holes. Solid and hollow marks align the layers.
1.85 × 1.85 mm pins; 2.0 × 2.0 mm holes. Designed space between pin and hole: 150 µm total, or 75 µm per side.
116 µm range across 96 pins. Compressible EPDM backing accommodates this variation during bonding.
3.8 mm height; 16° outer taper; 0.300 mm taper allowance. Each side narrows by 1.39 mm from bottom to top.
Up to 50 µL per well within the 9 mm grid and glass footprint.
Two-step skirt: 0.75 × 0.66 mm and 0.80 × 0.04 mm. Recessed adhesive-contact width: approximately 0.75–0.80 mm.
Matching masks and inserts: 1.0226 horizontal scale factor, or 2.26% enlargement, for curing at 100°C.
1 µm coating. A uniform film adds approximately 2 µm to ridge width; ridge height relative to the coated base remains approximately unchanged.
